newsitem.title: JAPAN: Kim Jong-il makes rare visit to truce village - KCNA.
newsitem.headline: Kim Jong-il makes rare visit to truce village - KCNA.

text.p: North Korea's leader-in-waiting Kim Jong-il visited the truce village of Panmunjom on Sunday for the first time in more than two decades, state media reported on Wednesday.
"Comrade Kim Jong-il, Supreme Commander of the Korean People's Army, inspected the Panmunjom mission of the KPA (Korea Workers' Party) on Sunday," the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

"He went up to the outpost where the enemy was in sight, looked round various units, barracks, bedrooms and logistic facilities and learned about how the soldiers were serving and living," KCNA said in a report monitored in Tokyo.
Panmunjom is the only crossing point along the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone that sealed the division of the Korean peninsula after the 1950-53 Korean War.

"He (Kim) showed high appreciation for the exploits of the soldiers, noting with great satisfaction that all of them were on alert duty in a responsible manner with a sharp eye on every movement of the enemy," KCNA said.
Kim, who has rarely appeared in public, last visited the border hamlet in 1972, according to the Tokyo-based Radiopress news agency.

Last week North Korea announced the temporary closure of its liaison office at the border village of Panmunjom in response to remarks by South Korean President Kim Young-sam that Seoul would never have a dialogue with the North.

The office was established in 1992 to promote civilian contacts, including cultural and government exchanges, and to facilitate family reunions after the prime ministers of North and South Korea signed a non-aggression treaty in 1991.

The Kim Jong-il, 54, who is supreme commander of North Korea's 1.1-million-strong military, has yet to be formally confirmed in the two key posts held by his late father Kim Il-sung -- general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
Kim Il-sung died in July 1994 after ruling the reclusive North for nearly five decades.
